title: Neurosymbolic Learning for Inference-Time Argumentation
claim: A claim's verdict can be computed from explicit, scored supporting and attacking arguments, yielding an uncertain outcome when evidence balances.
layout: 3 panels stacked vertically, attacks top, claim center, supports bottom, arrows converging inward
description: A vertical, symmetric diagram centered on a single blue-outlined Claim box reading 'Social media is more harmful than beneficial to society', annotated with base score τ(a_c)=0.50 and computed strength σ(a_c)=0.497. Above it, a pale red 'Attacks' band holds three red-bordered boxes (Arguments 1-3). Each contains an italic natural-language argument and a base score τ between 0.60 and 0.70. Below, a pale green 'Supports' band holds three green-bordered boxes (Arguments 4-6) with the same format and scores of 0.60-0.65. Thick red arrows curve down from the attack arguments into the claim. Green arrows curve up from the support arguments into it. The eye goes first to the central claim, then to the colored arrows and the scores.
caption: An example argumentative structure for a claim adapted from DEBATunE [ref]. Arguments 1-3 attack the claim and 4-6 support it. For claim/argument $x$, $\tau(x)$ is the base score and $\sigma(x)$ the argumentative strength computed by the DF-QuAD semantics [ref]. ITA classifies this claim as Uncertain as its strength is close to the midpoint of [0,1].
abstract: Claim verification is an important problem in high-stakes settings, including health and finance. When information underpinning claims is incomplete or conflicting, uncertain answers may be more appropriate than binary true or false classifications. In all cases, faithful explanations of the considerations determining the final verdict are crucial. We introduce inference-time argumentation (ITA), a trainable neurosymbolic framework for ternary claim verification in which a formal argumentation semantics giving the strength of claims and arguments is used both (i) to guide LLM training as models learn to generate arguments for and against claims and assign them base scores (representing intrinsic strengths) and (ii) to compute ternary (true/false/uncertain) predictions from generated, scored arguments. As a result, at training time, argument generation and scoring can be optimised according to the quality of the induced argumentative predictions. Moreover, at inference time, the final prediction is faithful, by construction, to the arguments and scores determining the verdict, rather than being justified by a potentially unfaithful post-hoc reasoning trace as in conventional reasoning models. We finally show that, on two datasets for ternary claim verification, ITA improves upon argumentative baselines and can perform competitively against non-argumentative direct-prediction baselines, while providing verdicts that are computed deterministically from explicit, inspectable argumentative structures. Our code, models and data are available at https://github.com/CLArg-group/inference-time-argumentation.
